title: The Benefits of Renovation Loans
paras: In a hot real estate market where conditions are generally favorable for home sellers, it’s not uncommon to hear about a home going under contract within a few days, or even a few hours. Of course, this creates a significant amount of frustration if you are actively searching for a new home.

The Fear of Missing Out is real, especially for those who have experienced the pain of missing out on the home of their dreams. Sometimes, it simply isn’t possible to make an offer fast enough, or keep pace with the frenzy of a multiple offer situation as prices skyrocket.

The inventory of homes with updated interiors and a reasonable price point is often going to be somewhat low in established, sought-after neighborhoods. A renovation loan could be the best possible solution for a buyer with budget constraints and a favorite neighborhood in mind. Renovation loans offer a wealth of advantages for buyers, such as:
- Less competition for available properties in great neighborhoods,
- The chance to customize updates, colors and amenities according to your individual tastes and preferences, and
- Better interest rates compared to credit cards or home equity lines.
The pool of buyers with interest in homes that need renovating is much smaller compared to homes that are in great condition. This results in a stronger, more relaxed negotiating position for buyers.

With a renovation loan, the funds that are needed to bring the home up to date are set aside at closing, into a trust account, and then rolled into the entire loan amount. The contractor in charge of the renovations has the authority to draw funds out of the trust at specified intervals (informally known as the draw) in order to pay for his/her fees and the cost of materials.

The savings that can be achieved with a renovation loan versus financing through credit cards or other forms of credit can be substantial. This makes renovation loans an extremely viable, attractive course of action for buyers who want to live in a specific location but do not have the requisite funds to cover an extensive home remodeling project out of pocket.

The process typically begins with a buyer finding a home that meets most of their expectations, yet needs work to repair some of the major systems. For a buyer in this situation, the first step would be to contact their mortgage broker to let that person know that they are interested in applying for a renovation loan.

The next step for the buyer is to contact the licensed general contractor of their choice, to tour the property with them and create a quote for the desired updates and the necessary repairs. At this point, it is advisable to have your real estate agent along with you. That individual can help you evaluate your options, decide on a course of action, and create a market value analysis of the home’s current and future value based on recent comparable sales.

The loan application has to include the quote from the contractor and the estimate of the home’s current market value, along with the estimated future value of the home after the repairs have been completed. There are many variables involved but the takeaway is that, as long as the value of the house after the repairs are completed is aligned with the value of comparable properties in the neighborhood with similar improvements, everything should be OK.

If not, the buyer will have to decide, “Do I want to bring more money to the closing table in order to ensure that the repairs I want to have done are completed?” Or, “Can I live with taking some of the items that I wanted to have done off the list, so that I can close on the property without having to pay as much out of pocket?”

Renovation loans are an excellent financing tool for buyers who want to live in a specific neighborhood and are fed up with losing out in multiple offer situations. While other buyers look to compete and have to spend well over asking price to get the home of their dreams, buyers who use renovation loans are often able to negotiate a significant rebate off the initial asking price.
note: Written for my real estate website when I was a licensed agent in Wilmington, North Carolina.

title: Four Questions for First Time Buyers
paras: If you are a first time buyer, you will likely have some questions about the process and timelines. Before you move forward on purchasing your first home, however, it is a good idea to ask yourself some important questions. Knowing the answers beforehand will help to simplify the process, minimize inconveniences and ensure your transaction closes successfully.

1) Where do you live now? This may seem obvious, but many first time buyers forget to let their agent know about their current living situation. Are you posted up on a friend’s couch or living with your parents? Are you tied to a lease? When does it expire? It’s important to know the answers prior to embarking on the negotiations, as the closing date will be crucial to everyone involved.

2) How quickly do you want to move? It is vital to answer this question immediately and pass your answer on to everyone involved in your home purchase transaction. Many first time buyers do not realize there are a fairly large number of people involved in the average transaction and many chess pieces that have to be successfully managed in order to ensure your transaction closes on time. Communicating the pertinent information to everyone involved, which can include loan officers, closing attorneys, home sellers, insurance agents and home inspectors, is an essential strategy for success.

3) Is anyone helping you? Are you buying your first home on your own? Or will your parents or a family member be helping you? If you will be receiving assistance in the form of a down payment, cash or a co-signer, it is very important to let your agent, attorney and loan officer know immediately. It will also be very helpful to let your real estate agent know if the people helping you will have to approve your decisions or if they will just be a silent partner in the transaction. This is especially important if you want to move quickly, decrease hassles and save time for everyone.

4) Where is the money coming from? Many first time buyers want to start shopping before they have been preapproved for a loan. This is a bad idea for the simple fact that it’s very disappointing to find out the home of your dreams is out of your price range. If your parents or someone else will be co-signing, providing cash to purchase, or giving down payment funds, it’s vital to let everyone involved in the transaction know about it, as there are very specific rules and procedures for wiring, handling and managing the money that will have to be performed in order to make sure the deal closes successfully.

Being proactive is the key to having a positive and hassle-free transaction experience. It is never a good thing to have to extend a closing date, as this can cost you extra money, or develop a creative solution for a problem that could have been prevented if all of the relevant information had been communicated and all of the needs identified at the outset of the process.
note: Written for my real estate website when I was a licensed agent in Wilmington, North Carolina.

title: Garden Club and Hobby Shop Make a Retirement Community Unique
paras: This June we are hosting an open house to showcase our Garden Club and Hobby Shop, two amenities that consistently top the list of favorites for our residents. Both are completely free for the residents to use and each one exemplifies the community’s focus on creating a comfortable, pleasant environment.

“It’s the people here that make the difference,” said Tom, Director of the Garden Club. “Everyone here had such a diverse and interesting career. You never know who you will meet when you go to dinner.”

Tom, who taught at a university, is explaining why he and his wife Ann decided to relocate here after spending 44 years in the Washington, D.C. area. “We are truly one big, happy family,” he adds, settling into a chair underneath an umbrella.

Tom helps in keeping the Garden Club’s 24 active members organized and ensures adequate supplies are on hand. He said one of his chief concerns in leaving his home for a Life Plan Community was having outdoor space to roam and a place to get his hands dirty in the garden. “Now all I have to worry about is what to do with all these tomatoes, blueberries, potatoes and cucumbers,” he joked.

This concern about having outdoor space to plant flowers and vegetables is the reason why the Garden Club was first established and why it continues to bear the name of the resident who petitioned the board to set aside a place for the residents 10 years ago. With status as a nonprofit, the board is always looking for new ways to reinvest the community’s earnings back into refining the services and amenities it provides for its residents.

As a result, there is now a spacious, wheelchair-accessible garden area that is set on approximately a half acre of land. It is completely surrounded by a privacy fence to ward off deer and other critters attracted by the aroma of the sweet smelling flowers and vegetables. A variety of plot sizes are available, from 20’ by 20’ and 10’ by 20’ ground plots, to raised beds and table gardens, for those who have trouble squatting or spending extensive periods of time on their knees.

Tom is considering polling the members about dividing the 20’ by 20’ plots. “They are almost too big,” he laughs. “And we want to make sure there is space for everyone.” Each of the plots has access to running water and a shed for storing tools. There are even two large compost bins for the residents to share organic fertilizer. The grounds and maintenance department helps with weed control and mulching, and operations are facilitated by a memorial fund specifically set aside for the Garden Club.

A quick stroll through the garden and it’s easy to see why so many works of art were inspired by the beauty put on display by the natural world. One of those unique artists with a talent for replicating the complexity found in nature is resident Walt, who can often be found in the woodworking and hobby shop, whittling away at a block of wood. Looking at a shell with tinges of red that he recently carved from a box elder tree, it is surprising to learn the red tones are actually produced by a stress reaction the trees have to a specific type of fungus. All of Walt’s works have a shine that looks as if he’s applied a protective coat of polyurethane. In reality this comes from many, many hours of his time sanding the wood, until he finishes with a 12,000 grit sand paper and calls it done.

Fellow Craftsmen Hank and Ray are equally talented. Ray is the go-to guy in the community when furniture needs to be repaired, refurbished or simply created from scratch to the highest standards of quality and style. Hank is the artisan responsible for crafting some really intricate and cool nut crackers, which take about 20 to 25 hours each to produce.

What the guys have in common is a focus on helping others, so each piece is either donated to a local church or sold in the gift shop at a nearby care center to fund the operations there. Another common element is an appreciation for the simple fact the shop is there and filled with every tool imaginable. A relief in not having to leave anything behind is a bond they share with the members of the Garden Club. Owning a home takes work. Part of the reward is the freedom to have a garden or a workshop. Here, we constantly look for new ways to ensure our residents have access to all the comforts of home, plus world-class health care and resort-like amenities, along with the sense of being free from the drudgery of interior and exterior home maintenance.
note: Sponsored content written for the marketing director of a nonprofit continuing care retirement community. Names have been changed.

title: Chef’s Demo Showcases Quality, Diversity of Food
paras: When I point out that having a chance to sample a variety of fine cuisine is one of the best parts about working here, it is not a surprise for many people. For those who are unfamiliar with our community, the assumption is that residents and staff have access to a cafeteria, not a restaurant.

This could not be farther from the truth, however, and luckily for me, dispelling the notion is as easy as…avoiding an obvious pun. It is as simple as inviting potential residents to experience firsthand the incomparable culinary talents of our executive chef and pastry chef, which is exactly what we did recently during an exclusive, four-course demonstration.

Were the menu available to me at the time of this writing, it would certainly make for a high-quality ingredient for use in the article. That is not the case, and the fact the menu is not currently available is indicative of the exceptional quality standards in place at the restaurant, where the emphasis is on creating a farm-to-table experience and many of the menu items are constantly changing.

To put it simply, the menu here was designed to be as fresh and vibrant as our residents. Our residents are what make our community great. They bring a variety of life experiences, tastes and preferences to the table, so it just made sense that our menu would need to be as diverse as they are.

Incorporating locally-sourced ingredients of the highest possible quality, the menu here is a tasty fusion of a variety of different styles. There are four new specials every day and the menu changes every week based on the preferences of our residents and what is currently available from the local markets.

The restaurant offers Certified Angus Beef and a new Catch-of-the-Day, every day. The menu is dynamic and fluid but the favorite mainstays that many are accustomed to seeing are always available. This makes our menu an effective blend of the adventurous and the tried-and-true.

Chef Mark is far from the stereotype of the angry chef or Soup Nazi. In fact, he is patient and humble, willing to listen to feedback or seek out the preferences of our residents. Chef Mark understands that many of our residents are not Southerners, and that the ones who are from the South are always willing to try new things. This is why he characterizes his kitchen as regional, with a twist—something that is never boring and truly unlimited in its appeal.

One of the coolest things about Chef Mark is that he invites the residents to bring in their favorite recipes, so that he and the staff can prepare them for everyone. The preparation and enjoyment of food is a common, universal thread. It brings people together in ways that are impossible to describe.

Being able to share a family favorite that has been carefully refined, tested and proven over the generations is something that our residents love. Many of our residents would like to have everyone who lives here over for dinner sometime, but the cost and the clean-up prevents that from happening. Having Chef Mark prepare and serve a traditional family recipe is similar to having everyone over for dinner, with none of the downside.

It is also worth noting that our residents are encouraged to share recipes and favorite foods from all over the world. Many of our residents are extremely well-traveled, and it has become a challenge, hobby and a source of pride for them to find something new, exciting and adventurous for the chef to create.

Of course, this creates a plethora of opportunities for social engagement, a veritable smorgasbord of social interaction, something that is well known to enrich people’s lives and foster a sense of community. We believe that our restaurant sets us apart from other Life Plan Communities, and we invite you to take a private tour or sign up for our next Chef’s Demo and experience the difference.
note: Sponsored content written for the marketing coordinator of a nonprofit continuing care retirement community. Names have been changed.

title: What Does Continuing Care Actually Mean?
paras: As the marketing director of a continuing care retirement community, dispelling the myths about continuing care retirement communities is something I do on a daily basis. The concept of continuing care is simply about providing a complete, all-inclusive package of amenities, benefits and services that are designed to fit into each phase of our residents’ lives.
It’s a principle that has guided us for more than two decades and it’s been a big part of our success as the first and only not-for-profit Continuing Care Retirement Community in the area.

Ensuring that our residents have priority access to health care throughout their lives is a key component of this. With an emphasis on matching our services to the changing needs of our residents, we offer 30 days of temporary care every year at no additional cost, starting from day one.

To deliver exceptional value and added peace of mind, we provide our residents with the opportunity to use a nearby health center and an assisted living facility should they ever need it. Both are known as premier health care providers in the area.

Of course, providing a complete package of amenities and services isn’t just about delivering the highest standard of health care available in the area. It’s about providing our residents with a worry-free lifestyle that includes weekly housekeeping and linen services, building maintenance, a 24-hour security staff and emergency response system, and a host of dining options.

Making sure our residents get the most out of their retirement is paramount to what we do. After all, continuing care is about taking care of the individual as a whole. Keeping that in mind, we make every effort possible to support the physical, social, emotional and spiritual well-being of our residents. We feel that doing so is an essential element of any continuing care program.

To that end we provide the residents of our community, which spans over 60 acres, with access to a fitness center with an indoor pool, salon services, a library, woodworking shop, garden area and artists’ studio. The expansion of our community is particularly exciting. Our beautiful new apartment homes opened in January of this year; a new auditorium and a wellness center with a saltwater pool will be open soon. We are also excited about the new bar and bistro that will be completed this summer.

If this were a conversation with a potential resident, this is where the issue of costs and entrance fees would come up. The entrance fee has earned a negative reputation that is grounded in a misconception. The actual fact is that 50 to 90 percent of all the entrance fees are returned. Residents here can rest easy in the knowledge that they will always have a place to live in our community—even if their income runs out.

Many of our potential residents don’t know that a portion of the entrance fee and the monthly costs are usually tax deductible. Add to that the fact that we provide our residents with a 25 percent discount at the health center, and the result is the peace of mind that comes from having priority access to the best healthcare in the area.
note: Advertorial written for the marketing director of a nonprofit continuing care retirement community, 2015.

title: Six Ways Bad Credit Can Ruin Your Life
paras: Okay, using the word ruin in terms of what a bad credit score can do to your life may be a bit of an overstatement. It is probably more accurate to say that bad credit can produce a nasty hiccup, necessitate a detour, or create a pothole on the road of life.

The subject came up recently when I was conversing with an older friend of mine, a home owner with several investment properties, a vacation home and a number of classic cars that were all purchased with cash. She had a simple question: “Why should I care whether or not I have good credit? I am definitely not trying to buy any more property.”

Most people understand that there is a need for a good credit score if seeking to obtain financing for a home. This is a situation in which having bad credit could cost you thousands or tens of thousands. Rest assured that lenders will thoroughly review your credit score and credit history during the mortgage application process. The worst case scenario is that your application for a loan could be denied if you have poor credit.

The other ways that bad credit can seriously impede your quality of life and drastically reduce your ability to be financially solvent are not quite as obvious. The list below contains a number of items that can get pricey or unattainable if your credit is less than positive.

- Credit cards – Interest rates on credit cards can range between seven percent and 36 percent. A good credit score can land you anywhere from 10 percent to 19 percent. With a bad credit score, the baseline interest rate can start at 22 percent and go up from there. This can make a huge impact, especially if you carry a balance.

- Car insurance – It is a surprise for many people to learn that insurance carriers in 47 states review an applicant’s credit score before deciding on a rate. The result is that you could have higher than average rates for years to come. Certain carriers may not even approve you for insurance coverage at all, if your credit score is extremely low.

- Searching for employment – Believe it or not, it is legal for a potential boss to analyze your credit report, as long as you approve it in writing. This type of information can be used for the basis of making decisions about hiring, and it’s permissible under the Fair Credit Reporting Act. After all, many types of employers, such as banks, jewelry stores, credit card companies, etc., face a significant amount of risk from theft, so it is easy to see their logic in deeming a candidate unworthy because of a credit score. However, some states have laws that limit the use of credit information in the hiring process.

- Cell phone plans – Similar to car insurance providers, cell phone companies will check your credit prior to activating their service. If you have poor credit, it’s possible that you will pay more each month for a phone or plan.

- Car loans – Without a good credit score, it may be difficult to secure financing for a car. Those who are able to get a loan with a bad credit score could end up paying up to two percentage points more than someone with stellar credit.

It is worthwhile to point out that, even if your credit is less than perfect, it may be possible to obtain financing for a home. Also, there are occasionally small issues or discrepancies on a credit report that can be resolved with something as trivial as a phone call. Taking care of these can make an individual’s credit score jump immediately.

title: Proven Techniques for Protecting Your Identity
paras: The annual gathering of receipts, W2s and 1099s and the filing of taxes is bad enough. But getting a message from the IRS that someone has already filed under your name has the potential to make any day go from bad to worse.

This form of identity theft occurs when a criminal acquires an individual’s social security number for the purpose of filing a fraudulent tax return. Though certainly not the only form of identity theft, it has been among the most popular in recent years, and this makes it a common cause of concern and conversation, especially during tax time.

Historically, the most popular choice for criminals who specialize in this segment has been to steal personal information such as social security numbers, dates of birth, home towns, first pets, etc., in the hopes of opening a new credit card or accessing an existing account. The companies that have built a business around monitoring and protecting individuals from identity theft sometimes make it seem as if the problem is a common occurrence.

The reality of the situation is that identity theft only affected a little over six percent of Americans last year, according to a study by Javelin Strategy and Research. Those who were unlucky enough to be a part of that crowd might have been happy or at least surprised to find out that it is most often the banks and credit card companies that have to eat the costs of identity theft and fraud, since the account holder’s liability is usually limited in the terms and conditions.

This does not mean it would be a good idea to be careless with your personal information. Instead of paying for an expensive monthly service, however, it could be worthwhile to explore the following easy, do-it-yourself techniques for protecting your identity:

- Opt out from pre-screened credit offers. Tell the Consumer Credit Reporting Companies you don’t want to receive offers of credit based on your information. Visit www.optoutprescreen.com or call 1–888–567–8688.

- Register at Do Not Call. Let the telemarketers know you would prefer not to hear from them. Many people do not realize that mobile phone numbers can also be added to the National Do Not Call Registry: www.DoNotCall.gov, or 888-382-1222.
- Take your name off direct mail lists. Visit www.dmachoice.org to request to have your name removed from Direct Mail Association mailing lists.

- Monitor credit scores and place alerts if necessary. It is a good idea to monitor your credit report and score through a free credit reporting service and/or one of the major credit reporting bureaus, such as Equifax, TransUnion or Experian. It’s also possible to place a fraud alert on your name if you think your identity has been compromised. Visit www.Equifax.com, www.TransUnion.com, or www.Experian.com for more information.

- Review Social Security data. Keep an eye on your benefits and earnings statement from the Social Security Administration, and ensure your number hasn’t been used by someone else: www.ssa.gov/mystatement.

title: Strategies for Saving Money When Refinancing
paras: With interest rates as low as they are, I have been getting lots of questions from home owners interested in refinancing their mortgage. This is certainly not surprising, considering the average interest rate for a 30-year fixed rate loan is around 3.27 percent, as of the date of this writing.

Of course, that can vary significantly according to a borrower’s income or financial situation. Similar to many other aspects of business and major life decisions, there are many variables involved with a refinance. This is why it’s key to start the process from a position of knowledge instead of uncertainty.
With that in mind, here are some questions that my clients frequently have for me, along with some valuable tips for saving money when refinancing a home.

- Don’t restart the clock – Doing a refinance to cash in on lower interest rates doesn’t necessarily mean that you have to get another 30-year loan. Many lenders these days have flexible guidelines that allow them to create a new loan and deed of trust for a differing number of years than the traditional 15-year and 30-year formats. If that is not an option, then a good course of action is to make an additional payment on the principal each month. This will shorten the payoff period and make a substantial difference over the long-term.

- Avoid paying closing costs – Seeking the lowest interest rate possible can actually result in significantly higher costs. In many cases a borrower’s lower-interest-rate option is accompanied by a large amount of points and fees, while the borrower’s slightly higher-interest-rate option has no fees and can even include additional rebate funds. Understanding that it is not unheard of for a borrower to spend up to $7,000 buying a lower interest rate, it is easy to see why opting for a loan with a slightly higher rate is a great choice for most situations. It may seem counterintuitive to think that a lower rate and a lower payment can cost more over the long-term, but that is the reality of the situation when closing costs are a factor.

- Choose a fixed rate – It’s not a good idea to get a loan product that includes a floating interest rate, with the hope that rates will fall in the future. There is no guarantee that rates will fall and if economic storm clouds suddenly began to form the interest rates and costs could increase dramatically.

- Shop around – Turning to friends, family and your social network for guidance regarding their favorite financial institution or mortgage broker is always worthwhile. It is important to note, however, that each inquiry from a creditor can reduce your credit score by two to five points. To increase the chance that several inquiries might only count as one, make sure to have your shopping and all of the inquiries performed in a 15-day time period.

- Get a second, and third opinion – Don’t give up if a lender tells you no. It is not uncommon for lenders to have different guidelines regarding eligibility. If it gets to the point where you have basically received the same answer from at least three sources, however, it may be time to ask for help identifying a solution to your credit issues.

title: Save on Cooling and Heating with Dual Zone HVAC Systems
paras: Remember Bugs Bunny and how he would occasionally say, “This means war?” Turning the thermostat up or down by a degree can certainly feel like an act of aggression. This is because, in many homes, especially split-level homes, someone is too hot, someone is too cold and no one is happy.

Even in a home with adequate central air conditioning, mom or dad may find the temperature to be fine in the kitchen or living room, but the basement game room might be so frigid the daughter has to find sweaters for her friends to wear. Upstairs, their son is visiting from college and actually wanting to study at his desk, yet the desk is so hot that he has trouble concentrating. This is a house that might benefit from a zoned HVAC system.
What is a zoned HVAC system?

A zoned HVAC (Heating, Ventilation and Air Conditioning) system allows the homeowner to set different temperatures in different parts or “zones” of the house. Instead of only using one thermostat for the entire house, each zone can be regulated with its own thermostat, fully customized to the preference of the user. A zone can be as small as a room, as large as an entire floor, or an addition to the house.
How does zoning work?

A common misconception is that, to have multiple zones, multiple systems must be installed. In a home with an existing forced air heating and cooling system (and one thermostat), however, it may be possible to install an automatic damper system into the ductwork, to divide the home into zones.

The better way to set up a zoned HVAC system is with ductless mini-split units. Though these units come in a variety of styles and models, it is basically just a small heating/cooling unit that is mounted high on the wall (or to the ceiling). This indoor air-handling unit (evaporator) is hooked up to an outdoor compressor/condenser unit. Several indoor units can be hooked up to one outdoor unit, and each indoor unit is controlled with its own thermostat.
Reasons for switching to a zoned HVAC system

Ductless mini-splits are a great solution for a newly constructed house, and a good retrofit for houses with non-ducted heating systems. They also work well for new additions to a house that lack ductwork or separate buildings like a garage or shed converted into offices or hobby rooms. Why might you want to look into installing some ductless mini-splits?
- Solves the multi-level home heating/cooling problem.
- Balances the temperature in homes where one side of the house gets more solar heat than the other side.
- To only heat/cool the parts of the home in use.
- Avoid installing ductwork in new house additions /separate buildings/studios/garages.

Considering that a variety of factors, such as solar heat, inadequate sealing or a lack of insulation can cause the temperature within a home to vary significantly from room to room, a multiple zone HVAC system can amount to a substantial return on investment, both in costs and comfort.

title: How to Reduce Indoor Allergens
paras: Spring is officially here, and for those of us with a sensitivity to pollen and other allergens, the joy of the season can be somewhat muted, to say the least. Sure, the flowers are beautiful and the warmer weather is wonderful, but who wants to deal with allergy attacks or respiratory infections?

It’s impressive to witness the daily accumulation of pollen on our cars, sidewalks and streets, and most of us realize that it is necessary to agricultural production; however it is worth pointing out that all that pollen does not stay outside.
Every time someone opens a door or a window, walks inside with shoes on or lets a pet come indoors, pollen becomes an uninvited guest. And pollen is not even one of the worst of the indoor allergens.

Mold, dust mites and pet dander can also have a negative impact on indoor air quality. It may also not be a surprise to learn that cockroaches can cause allergic reactions in people. There are a variety of other culprits that can produce indoor allergens, such as:
- Soft furniture and bedding
- Wall-to-wall carpet
- Indoor plants
- Stuffed toys
- Mattresses that aren’t in allergy covers
So how can these contaminants, which can absolutely cause and/or exacerbate a variety of health issues, be controlled?
1. Purchase a high-quality air filter. Using a filter that has been certified as asthma and allergy friendly can result in an almost 98 percent reduction of allergen particles.

2. Reduce humidity. Maintaining a relatively low level of humidity can drastically inhibit the proliferation of dust mites and mold. A few strategies for decreasing humidity would be to purchase a dehumidifier, run the air conditioner on recirculate, and keep the doors and windows closed.

3. Avoid thick carpeting; keep surfaces clean and uncluttered. Basically, any step that makes it easier to dust and/or run the vacuum is a good idea. It is important to not just brush the dust away with a feather duster or cloth, however. Instead, use a damp microfiber cloth to trap the dust. Vacuuming once or twice a week is also a good idea, but it is important to use one that has been certified as asthma and allergy friendly.

4. Keep pets out of the bedroom. For those with an allergy to animal dander, it’s not advisable to have a pet with feathers or fur. If you already have a pet, keeping them out of the bedroom, washing and disinfecting their favorite toys and furniture can be effective strategies for reducing the amount of dander in the air.
There are many other strategies that can be implemented to help reduce the amount of indoor air contaminants inside a home.
note: Written for a heating and air conditioning company. Client names and contact details have been removed, and prices are as of the original publication.

title: Are Service Contracts Worth the Investment?
paras: If you are like me and subscribe to the wisdom of Ben Franklin, who famously uttered in 1736 that, “An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure,” it’s likely you will agree that purchasing a service contract is a wise investment. Of course, keeping the system from breaking in the first place is better than having to order parts and wait for them to arrive, all while experiencing the onslaught of summer humidity that is iconic to the South.

It is worth pointing out that the average repair cost for an HVAC system ranges between $150 and $650, with the labor alone for technicians averaging between $75 and $150 per hour. With that in mind, it’s easy to see why many home owners view service contracts as an effective strategy for reducing costs.

The numbers referenced above are just a baseline scenario. In the heat of the summer or in the cold of the winter, if something happens to the system over the weekend and you want it repaired, the visit from the technician will carry along with it an emergency service call fee.

The cost of joining a maintenance plan would more than likely pay for itself after just one emergency or holiday visit when a repair was necessary. A few of the maintenance and prevention measures that are covered in a maintenance plan visit are listed below:
- Inspect the system and ductwork
- Check exposed equipment and pipes for leaks
- Inspect thermostat condition and operation
- Check heat strips, defrost controls and reversing valve of the heat pump
- Start the capacity compressor and compressor fans to check recommended and actual MFD ratings
- Inspect the indoor and outdoor coils
- Add algae tabs in the drain pan
- Test compressor protection device
- Inspect condenser and overflow switch
- Check current draw of compressor and the refrigerant operating pressure

There are also many intangibles that could result from purchasing a service contract.
